quickAnswer: Lancaster has the 2nd-highest share of bottled or tank gas heating among the 50 towns we serve (12.7% of homes, ACS 2022), on top of 60.0% on fuel oil. Only 9.0% use utility gas, so most replacement decisions here involve a delivered fuel.
body: ## Two delivered fuels and very little pipeline gas

According to the Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS), 380 Lancaster homes (12.7%) heat with bottled or tank gas. That is the 2nd-highest share of the 50 towns Mass HVAC serves; the middle town sits at 4.5%. Fuel oil heats 1,790 homes (60.0%, 10th-highest), electricity heats 407 (13.7%), and wood heats 82 (2.8%). Utility gas heats just 269 homes, or 9.0%, which ranks 48th of 50 against 41.9% for the middle town.

In practice, a failed boiler or furnace in a house like these usually opens one of three questions: oil for oil, a switch to another tank fuel, or a heat pump. Oil and propane both arrive by delivery and sit in a tank on the property, so the tank, the venting and the age of the existing equipment all enter the decision.
## The mother town and its oldest houses

Lancaster was incorporated in 1653 and is the oldest town in Worcester County. It calls itself the "mothertown" of eastern central Massachusetts: Harvard, Bolton, Leominster, Clinton, Berlin, Sterling and part of West Boylston were all formed from its original territory. The buildings reflect that long history. 725 homes (23.7%) date from 1939 or earlier, the 7th-highest share of the 50 towns, and 61.7% of all homes were built before 1980. The median home was built in 1966, against 1975 for the middle town. The town covers 28.2 square miles, of which 27.7 is land.

Houses of that age were often built with less insulation than a current code home, and some have ductwork added later or none at all. Heat loss varies a lot from one old house to the next, so the heating load is worked out house by house instead of from the size of the unit in the cellar.
The housing is not all old. 649 homes (21.3%) went up in 2000 or later, and 145 of those (4.7%) since 2010. Newer houses tend to be tighter, so their needs differ from a pre-1940 farmhouse's.
## Town wells, private wells and sewer streets

Town wells supply most of Lancaster's water, while properties on or north of Lunenburg Road rely on private wells, and only some streets, largely those nearest Clinton and Main Street out to Route 117, are on the sewer district.
## What National Grid means for heat pump rebates

National Grid is the electric delivery utility. For supply, residents can use the supplier National Grid contracts with, choose their own, or join the town's municipal aggregation program. National Grid customers can generally look to Mass Save for heat pump rebates, provided the house is weatherized first. The [heat pump page](/cities/lancaster/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) has the amounts and conditions.
## Owners, renters and home values

Owners occupy 2,458 of the town's 2,981 occupied homes (82.5%), while 523 households (17.5%) rent. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $398,200, 45th-highest of the 50 towns and well under the middle town's $579,150. Detached houses make up 79.9% of the housing stock, against 76.7% for the middle town. Vacancy is 2.4%, or 72 of the 3,053 housing units, against 3.6% for the middle town. Only 17.5% of households rent, a bit above the middle town's 16.4%.

faq.q: Is natural gas an option for my Lancaster house?
faq.a: Only a small share of homes use it. Utility gas heats 269 Lancaster homes, 9.0% of the total, against 41.9% for the middle town. Whether a main runs past your address is a question for the gas company. Where none does, the usual choices are oil, propane or a heat pump.

faq.q: Why is propane so common in Lancaster?
faq.a: We can report the number but not the reason. The Census Bureau counts 380 Lancaster homes heated with bottled or tank gas, 12.7%, which is 2nd of the 50 towns. For a homeowner, the practical point is that propane and oil are both delivered fuels, so comparing their running costs with a heat pump is worth doing.

faq.q: Which part of Lancaster has the oldest houses?
faq.a: The sheet does not break the housing down by neighborhood, so we cannot say. It does show that 725 homes date to 1939 or earlier and 611 to 1960 through 1979, and houses from different bands tend to differ in insulation, so a heating load assessment of your own house is the reliable guide.

faq.q: Will the older housing in Lancaster affect what system I choose?
faq.a: It can. With the median home built in 1966, insulation, air leakage and ducts vary widely from house to house. Equipment sized from the old unit may be too large or too small, so the heating load comes first and the unit second.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Fuel oil heats 1,790 Lancaster homes and bottled gas 380, while only 269 sit on a gas main. A replacement here often starts with a choice between oil, propane and a heat pump, then moves on to venting and sizing.
body: ## Replacing a boiler when the gas main is the exception

Lancaster ranks 10th of 50 for fuel oil, and the middle town of the 50 sits at 36.5%. Add 380 homes on tank gas, 407 on electricity, 82 that burn wood and 53 on other fuels or coal, and the town splits into several heating camps rather than one. Utility gas serves 269 homes, which is why a switch to natural gas is a smaller part of the picture here than the middle town's 41.9% would suggest.
### Oil for oil, propane, or a heat pump

Each path asks for different work. Oil for oil keeps the tank and chimney, though an old flue liner may need attention. Oil to propane is a conversion, with a new burner or boiler, gas piping and a regulator. A heat pump removes the burner, and in many houses a boiler stays in place for the coldest days.
### The permit step

Anyone replacing gas or propane equipment needs a licensed plumber or gas fitter, the only trades allowed to pull a gas permit in Massachusetts, and the job normally closes with an inspection. The building department can say how it handles the paperwork.
### The house behind the boiler

Radiators, baseboard runs and narrow ducts can outlast the boiler that feeds them. Many Lancaster houses predate 1980, so a new heat source has to suit whatever distribution system the old one left behind. Before a quote, the house's heating load is calculated, which beats trusting the old unit's label.
### Renters and the 68 F floor

Lancaster counts 523 renter households. For those households the state code sets a heating-season floor of 68 F between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m., dropping to 64 F overnight, and heat is the landlord's cost unless the lease says differently. Take this as general information, not legal advice.
### Heat out at night

Call (508) 786-8755. Emergency calls are taken around the clock, and the written estimate is free before work starts. For the numbers behind the town's housing, see the [Lancaster overview](/cities/lancaster).

faq.q: Can I change from oil to propane when my boiler fails?
faq.a: Often, yes, but it is a real conversion that involves a burner or boiler, gas piping, a tank arrangement and a permit. Price it against a plain oil replacement and against a heat pump before deciding, because the cheapest first step is not always the cheapest over the years.

faq.q: Is a wood stove enough as a backup heat source?
faq.a: Wood is the main heat for 82 Lancaster homes, 2.8%, so it is a real heat source for some owners. As a backup it works only if the chimney and flue are sound, so have them inspected before relying on it through a long cold spell.

faq.q: How do I know whether to repair or replace?
faq.a: A single failed part on a young boiler is usually worth repairing. A cracked heat exchanger, repeated breakdowns or equipment well past its expected life point toward replacement. A written estimate lets you compare both routes side by side.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Detached houses are 79.9% of Lancaster's housing, so most cooling jobs are single-family. Central air can suit houses with usable ducts, and ductless mini-splits can suit the rest.
body: ## Cooling a town of detached houses

The ACS counts 2,440 detached houses and 234 attached townhouse units among Lancaster's 3,053 housing units. Another 379 homes sit in multi-unit buildings: 145 in two-unit buildings, 79 in buildings of three or four units and 155 in buildings of five or more. There are no mobile homes. The building type shapes the cooling plan more than the size of the town does.
### A condenser and ducts

A detached house usually has yard space for an outdoor condenser. Central cooling then depends on ducts, and many older homes were built before central air was common, so the routes can be short on room. Running new ones may mean opening walls and ceilings. A window unit can cool a single room, though it blocks a window and can lose its seal over time.
### When ductless fits

A mini-split uses an outdoor unit and a small indoor head joined by a thin line set. It can serve an addition, a finished attic or a house with hot-water baseboard, and one head may be enough for a single stubborn room. The same equipment also heats, which links to the [heat pump page](/cities/lancaster/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### The 407 electric-heat homes

Electricity heats 407 Lancaster homes, 13.7%, the 17th-highest share of the 50 towns. In a house heated by baseboard resistance, a heat pump can take over cooling from window units and part of the winter load as well.
### Newer houses, other loads

The 649 homes built in 2000 or later, about one in five, may already have ducts. Their cooling load can still differ from a 1966 house, the town's median year, because insulation and window area change from one era to the next.
### Oversized units

A bigger air conditioner is not a better one. An oversized unit cools the air fast and shuts off before it removes much humidity, leaving a cool but clammy house. Sizing comes from insulation, window area and orientation, not from the old unit.

faq.q: Can I add air conditioning to a Lancaster house with hot-water baseboard heat?
faq.a: Yes. With no ducts in the house, a ductless mini-split is the usual route. Each indoor head cools one area and the outdoor unit connects through a small opening in the wall. A visit shows whether one head or several would suit the layout and the rooms that run hottest.

faq.q: Should one heat pump replace the separate air conditioner?
faq.a: It can be, since one system both heats and cools. The answer depends on the fuel you burn now, the condition of the house and whether the rebate conditions fit. Compare the full yearly cost, not only the cooling side of the equipment.

faq.q: What can fail first on a weak central air system?
faq.a: Often something modest: a capacitor, a dirty coil or a slow refrigerant leak. A failed compressor in an old system is a different story and may point to replacement. A written estimate separates the cheap fixes from the costly ones before any work begins.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: National Grid delivers electricity in Lancaster, so Mass Save is the rebate path to check for a heat pump. With 1,790 homes on oil and 380 on propane, many owners have a delivered fuel to replace.
body: ## A heat pump against a delivered fuel

The 2026 Mass Save whole-home heat pump rebate pays by the ton and has a cap per home, and the house must be weatherized first. Confirm the terms at masssave.com, and see the [general heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) for the full conditions.
### Where the fuel switch is largest

Lancaster's 1,790 oil homes and 380 propane homes are the obvious candidates, because a heat pump displaces fuel that is trucked in and burned. The 269 homes on a gas main face a different comparison, and 407 electric-heat homes may gain from replacing baseboard with a heat pump. Lancaster's 60.0% oil share is well above the middle town's 36.5%. The 12.7% propane share is nearly three times the middle town's 4.5%, so propane customers form a larger group here than in most of the 50 towns.
### Age against the 2000 line

One of the ways a home passes the weatherization test is by being built in 2000 or later. In Lancaster that covers 649 homes, 21.3%. Everything else was built earlier, and 725 homes date to 1939 or before, so for most of the town an assessment and some air sealing may come first.
### Partial home, kept boiler
A home keeping its boiler for the coldest days falls under the partial-home rebate, $1,125 per ton. The whole-home route fits a house where the heat pump will carry the full load.
### Choosing a supplier

Lancaster has a municipal aggregation program, administered through Colonial Power Group. It sets who supplies the electricity, while National Grid keeps delivering it. Residents may also use the supplier National Grid contracts with, or sign with one of their own.
### Houses without ducts

A ductless system can serve a house with no ducts, which can be the case in older construction. The [cooling page](/cities/lancaster/air-conditioning-installation-repair) shows how mini-splits fit a detached house. Households on electric baseboard are the other group where a ductless system often replaces something less efficient.

faq.q: Do I qualify for the Mass Save whole-home rebate in Lancaster?
faq.a: You may if you are a National Grid customer, the equipment goes in during 2026, and the house passes the weatherization test. Many Lancaster houses predate 2000, so a Home Energy Assessment is a common first step. Confirm every condition at masssave.com before you order.

faq.q: Can a heat pump work alongside the oil boiler I already have?
faq.a: Yes. A partial-home setup lets the heat pump carry most of the year while the boiler handles the coldest stretch. In an oil house that may mean fewer deliveries even if the tank stays. Check the partial-home terms before choosing the size.

faq.q: Does the town's aggregation program change who delivers my power?
faq.a: No. The program, run with Colonial Power Group, affects only the supply side of your bill. National Grid still delivers electricity and still sets the rebate path. If you have signed with another supplier, the delivery utility is the same.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: With 60.0% of Lancaster homes on oil and 12.7% on propane, service here is mostly about burners, tanks and flues. A tune-up before the first cold snap beats an emergency call on a freezing night.
body: ## Service for tank-fed equipment

An oil boiler or furnace wants a cleaning once a year: burner, nozzle, filter and heat exchanger, plus a combustion test. Propane equipment has its own check of burner, venting and controls. Electric and heat pump households need coils, filters and refrigerant-side attention instead. Lancaster has households in every one of these groups, so a single town needs several kinds of visit.
### The oil visit

- Clean the burner and the boiler or furnace.
- Change the filter and the nozzle.
- Test combustion and inspect the flue.
### Propane, gas and wood
Propane and gas appliances get a flame, venting and connection check. Wood stoves and boilers warm 82 Lancaster homes, 2.8%, and their chimneys and flues are a separate inspection from the boiler's.
### Heat pumps and cooling

Mini-splits and central air need clean filters, coils and condensate drains, and a look at the outdoor unit. The 407 electric-heat homes in town are the likeliest to have this equipment running all year. Outdoor units also need a clear pad, free of leaves and snow.
### The age of what is being serviced

Lancaster's median house dates to 1966, and 611 homes come from 1960 through 1979 while 520 come from 1980 through 1999. Equipment in houses of those eras has often been replaced at least once, but the age of the unit, not the house, sets the schedule.
### Owners and landlords

Owners hold 2,458 households and renters hold 523. A landlord who has the boiler serviced ahead of the heating season is less likely to meet a no-heat call. Late summer is also the easiest time to book, and spring suits cooling checks.
### Signs to call about early

A new noise, a smell of oil or smoke, or short cycling, where a burner or compressor starts and stops every few minutes, should not wait for the next annual visit. See the [air quality page](/cities/lancaster/indoor-air-quality) for what a tune-up leaves out.

faq.q: How often should an oil system in Lancaster be cleaned?
faq.a: Yearly, ahead of the heating season. Skipping a year can let soot build up on the heat exchanger, which may cut efficiency and bring a breakdown during the coldest weeks. A visit in late summer leaves time to order parts if something is worn.

faq.q: Does a propane furnace need a yearly tune-up too?
faq.a: A yearly check is a sound habit. The technician looks at the burner, the venting, the controls and the gas connections, and reports anything worn. Lancaster ranks 2nd of 50 for propane heating, so there are many such systems that benefit from the same routine.

faq.q: Do heat pumps need maintenance as well?
faq.a: Yes, though it is lighter. Filters need cleaning, coils and drains need a look, and outdoor units need clearance from leaves and snow. Doing this once a year, ahead of the season you rely on the unit most, keeps small problems from becoming service calls.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Lancaster's housing spans 725 homes from 1939 or earlier to 145 built since 2010, so air problems differ: old houses leak and can be damp, newer ones are tight. Private wells north of Lunenburg Road matter if you add a humidifier.
body: ## Air in houses of very different ages

The ACS 2022 sorts Lancaster's housing into age bands: 548 homes (17.9%) from 1940 to 1959, 611 (20.0%) from 1960 to 1979, 520 (17.0%) from 1980 to 1999, 649 from 2000 on and 725 from 1939 or earlier. Each band has its own air story, and one house may hold more than one, since additions often differ from the original building. The 1940 to 1999 bands together make up most of the rest of the housing.
### Older houses

Gaps around windows, sills and attic floors let old houses exchange air with the outdoors. That can dilute some indoor pollutants, yet it also lets in dust, pollen and basement damp. Before renovating a very old house, have a qualified specialist test for lead paint or asbestos.
### Newer, tighter houses

The 145 Lancaster homes built since 2010 are likelier to be tight. A tight house holds moisture, cooking fumes and chemicals from furnishings unless ventilation is working, so a bathroom fan and range hood that vent outside matter more.
### Humidity

Winter air indoors is often dry, and summer brings humidity back. A humidifier tied to the system can ease dryness and a dehumidifier can tame a damp basement. Where a humidifier draws on a private well, mineral deposits can build up, so ask about upkeep before buying one.
### Filters and ducts
A better filter only helps if the blower can pull air through it. Duct cleaning is worth considering when ducts are visibly dirty or moldy, not as a routine chore.
### Combustion safety

Oil, propane and wood appliances should vent properly. Wood heat, used in 82 Lancaster homes, adds smoke and fine particles when a stove or flue is poorly vented or fed damp wood. and a carbon monoxide alarm on each floor is cheap protection. If one sounds, leave the house and call for help. The [tune-up page](/cities/lancaster/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) covers the burner side of this.

faq.q: Is my old Lancaster house likely to have worse air than a new one?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Old houses tend to leak, which helps ventilation but brings in dust and damp. Newer houses are tight, which holds in moisture and fumes. Both can be improved once the source of the problem is clear, and the fix is rarely the same for the two kinds of house.

faq.q: Do I need my ducts cleaned?
faq.a: Not automatically. Cleaning is worth considering when ducts are visibly dirty, moldy or were disturbed by a renovation or pests. Many houses never need it. Looking at the system first shows whether cleaning would help or whether a filter and a sealed return would do more.

faq.q: Does my water source matter for a humidifier?
faq.a: It can. Properties on or north of Lunenburg Road use private wells, and hard well water can leave mineral scale in a humidifier. Homes on town water are less likely to see the same buildup. Ask about pads, descaling and upkeep before you buy a unit.
